terraform-opentofu-advanced.core: Advanced Terraform/OpenTofu is about running the declarative plan/apply loop safely at scale: pinned providers, data sources instead of hardcoded IDs, versioned modules, stable for_each keys, explicit environment separation, locked remote state, assertions instead of tribal knowledge, and avoiding imperative provisioners.

first_principles.problem: Hello-world Terraform breaks under multiple people, environments and modules.

analogy.title: Blueprints for a city, not a shed
analogy.story: Standards, permits and inspections matter once many builders work on many buildings.
analogy.breaks: Cities evolve slowly; infra changes daily.

example.title: A production-ready service stack
flow: envs/prod with own S3 backend + lock
Calls versioned service module with for_each per service
AMI via data source, preconditions on arch

check.q: Why prefer for_each over count for collections?
check.a: Its key-based addresses stay stable when items are added or removed, avoiding destroy/recreate cascades.

terraform-advanced-state-strategy.core: State is the mapping between code and reality, and strategy is how you keep it safe and scalable. Use remote, locked, encrypted backends; split state into layers by lifecycle and owner; wire layers through narrow contracts; detect drift on a schedule; import legacy resources; refactor with moved blocks; and keep secrets out of state.

first_principles.problem: State mistakes cause outages, data loss and leaked secrets.

analogy.title: The land registry for your infrastructure
analogy.story: It records who owns which plot; it must be secure, divided into districts, and kept in sync with the ground.
analogy.breaks: Land rarely changes; infra drifts daily.

example.title: Healthy state estate
flow: Per-layer S3 keys with KMS and locking
Refactors via moved blocks in PRs

check.q: Why split one state file into layers?
check.a: To shrink blast radius and plan time, reduce lock contention, and align ownership with change frequency.

terraform-advanced-state-management.core: Scaling Terraform means escaping the monolithic state: split into stacks ordered as a downward-only hierarchy, break circular dependencies by extracting shared pieces, and migrate resources between states with moved, removed and import blocks, never destroying or double-managing real infrastructure.

first_principles.problem: A giant state is slow, risky and blocks every team.

analogy.title: Reorganising a warehouse into depots
analogy.story: Plan the routes, avoid depots waiting on each other, and move stock without losing any.
analogy.breaks: Stock is physical; state mistakes destroy real resources.

example.title: Monolith split
flow: Moved via removed + import in batches
example.outcome: state that scales with the org.

check.q: What verifies a successful state migration?
check.a: Zero-change plans in both the old and new stacks after the move.

terraform-custom-provider-development.core: Terraform is a plugin system: providers are Go binaries speaking gRPC to core. Writing one means modelling an API's resources as typed schemas with the Plugin Framework, implementing accurate CRUD (especially Read), proving it with acceptance tests against the real API, debugging with tflog and Delve, and publishing signed releases.

first_principles.problem: Systems without a provider are managed by tickets and scripts outside IaC.

analogy.title: Writing a driver for new hardware
analogy.story: The OS works once the driver translates its generic calls into the device's language.
analogy.breaks: Drivers run in-kernel; providers run as isolated processes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: DNS changes go through PR + plan like everything else.

check.q: Which CRUD method most affects drift detection?
check.a: Read, because it refreshes state from the API before every plan.

iac-abstractions-cdk-pulumi.core: CDK, CDKTF and Pulumi let you write infrastructure in real programming languages: classes, packages and tests for abstraction, while still producing declarative desired state. CDK builds a construct tree (L1/L2/L3) synthesised to CloudFormation; Pulumi's engine drives many clouds directly. Encode org standards as custom constructs, mind cross-stack coupling, and extend to any API with custom providers.

first_principles.problem: Configuration languages struggle with abstraction, reuse and testing.

analogy.title: Moving from forms to software
analogy.story: Forms are fine for a few fields; software lets you reuse logic, validate and test.
analogy.breaks: Software can do anything, which is a risk; keep synth deterministic.

example.title: Platform library
flow: StandardService L3 with alarms and IAM

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Consistent, tested infra with less code.

check.q: What's the key difference in how CDK and Pulumi deploy?
check.a: CDK synthesises CloudFormation templates and CloudFormation deploys them; Pulumi's engine calls cloud providers directly and tracks its own state.

cdk8s-kubernetes-as-code.core: cdk8s replaces walls of Kubernetes YAML with typed code. A client-side engine renders a construct tree into plain manifests; `cdk8s import` provides types for core APIs and CRDs; and constructs (cdk8s-plus and your own) encode standards such as probes and limits so services are declared in a few lines and deployed by any GitOps tool.

first_principles.problem: Duplicated, fragile YAML is hard to change consistently.

analogy.title: A mail merge for manifests
analogy.story: Write the template logic once and print every variant correctly.
analogy.breaks: Mail merge is text; cdk8s is typed objects.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Typed source, plain YAML in Git.

check.q: How does cdk8s fit with Argo CD?
check.a: cdk8s renders YAML in CI and commits it (or uses a plugin); Argo CD syncs those plain manifests to the cluster.

crossplane-k8s-infrastructure.core: Crossplane makes Kubernetes a universal control plane: providers turn cloud resources into CRDs reconciled continuously, and Compositions let platform teams publish simple self-service APIs that expand into compliant infrastructure. It complements rather than replaces Terraform: continuous and self-service versus planned and broad.

first_principles.problem: On-demand IaC leaves drift between runs and requires infra expertise from every team.

analogy.title: A thermostat with a simple menu
analogy.story: Pick 'comfortable' and the system keeps it that way.
analogy.breaks: Thermostats are simple; compositions need careful design.

check.a: Its controllers continuously compare desired specs with cloud state and correct any drift.

gitops-terraform-atlantis-flux.core: GitOps for Terraform makes Git the source of truth and automation the only applier. Atlantis posts plans and applies from PR comments with locks and approvals; the Flux tofu-controller reconciles Terraform from Git inside Kubernetes; and trunk-based directories with versioned modules make environment promotion an explicit, reviewable change.

first_principles.problem: Laptop applies are unreviewed, unaudited and conflict with each other.

analogy.title: A dual-signature bank workflow
analogy.story: Requests are logged, checked and executed by the system, never by one person alone.
analogy.breaks: Banks enforce by law; you enforce with branch protection.

check.q: What are the two core rules of IaC GitOps?
check.a: All changes go through Git pull requests, and only automation (not people) applies them.

stack-orchestration-terragrunt-spacelift.core: Splitting state creates an orchestration problem: boilerplate, dependency order and output passing. Terragrunt keeps configuration DRY and runs units as a DAG with dependency outputs (mocked for first runs), while SaaS platforms like Spacelift and HCP Terraform add remote runs, policies, drift detection and dependency-triggered pipelines.

first_principles.problem: Dozens of stacks are hard to configure, order and connect by hand.

analogy.title: A construction schedule
analogy.story: Crews know their order and get handed measurements from the crew before them.

example.title: New region bring-up
example.outcome: many stacks managed as one system.

check.q: What does terragrunt run-all apply do?
check.a: Applies every unit under the directory in dependency order, in parallel where the graph allows.

testing-infrastructure-as-code.core: IaC testing follows a pyramid of speed against realism: static analysis (fmt, validate, TFLint, Checkov) in seconds; plan analysis with OPA and Sentinel policies on the planned changes; module tests with terraform test; and integration tests that deploy, verify and destroy real infrastructure. Pipelines run the cheap layers on every push and the expensive ones on merge or nightly.

first_principles.problem: Untested IaC ships insecure or broken infrastructure.

analogy.title: Spell-check, editor, rehearsal
analogy.story: Each pass catches what the previous couldn't.

example.title: Pipeline outcome
flow: 90% of bugs caught by static + plan checks

check.q: Which test layer sees computed values but doesn't create resources?
check.a: Plan analysis: policies evaluating terraform show -json output.

policy-as-code-opa-sentinel-checkov.core: Policy as code replaces slow manual review with automated, consistent guardrails. Scanners like Checkov and Trivy give instant built-in coverage; OPA/Rego is a universal engine for plans, Kubernetes and APIs; Sentinel integrates tiered enforcement into HashiCorp platforms; and policies run in layers from IDE to runtime.

first_principles.problem: Manual review is either a bottleneck or a rubber stamp.

analogy.title: Mountain road guardrails
analogy.story: Drive fast; the rails stop you going over the edge.
analogy.breaks: Rails cover every bend; policies only cover written rules.

example.title: Org rollout
flow: Month 2: Rego for org rules on plans

check.q: Why roll policies out as advisory first?
check.a: To measure findings and fix false positives before blocking teams, building trust in the rules.

ansible-automation-basics.core: Ansible configures what infrastructure runs: agentless over SSH, desired state in YAML, idempotent modules. Inventories (ideally dynamic) define targets, playbooks list tasks, variables follow precedence, Jinja2 templates adapt configs, handlers restart only on change, roles organise reuse, tags focus runs, and Vault protects secrets.

first_principles.problem: Hand-configured servers drift and can't be rebuilt reliably.

analogy.title: A head chef's checklists
analogy.story: Every kitchen set up identically from tested checklists, with locked recipes for secret sauces.

check.q: How does Ansible differ from Terraform in purpose?
check.a: Terraform provisions infrastructure resources; Ansible configures software and settings on hosts.

immutable-infrastructure-packer.core: Immutable infrastructure treats servers as cattle: never modify in place, bake every change into a versioned image and replace instances. Packer builds images from HCL templates via temporary builders and provisioners; golden images carry hardening and agents from first boot; and an AMI lifecycle handles rebuilds, promotion channels, sharing and retirement.

first_principles.problem: In-place changes create unique, unreproducible, non-compliant servers.

analogy.title: Factory-built cars
analogy.story: Every car matches the tested model; upgrades mean new cars, not roadside repaints.
analogy.breaks: Cars are costly; instances are cheap to replace.

example.title: Weekly patch rollout
flow: Monday: Packer rebuild with latest patches
InSpec passes → publish to dev channel

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fleet fully patched weekly without SSH.

check.q: How do you deploy a patch in immutable infrastructure?
check.a: Build a new image with the patch, promote it, and replace running instances with ones launched from it.

legacy-config-management-migration.core: Legacy configuration management (Puppet, Chef, Salt, then Ansible) was built for long-lived pets, fighting drift by continuous convergence through agents or pushes. Each model trades setup cost, speed and enforcement differently. Migration to immutable infrastructure works best incrementally, reusing CM code inside Packer as a bridge and retiring runtime CM last.

first_principles.problem: Teams must decide what to do with aging CM estates in a cloud-native world.

analogy.title: From classic-car maintenance to a rental fleet
analogy.story: Keep using your mechanics' know-how to prep rental cars until you no longer need the workshop.
analogy.breaks: Cars don't have code; CM code can be directly reused.

example.title: Two-year roadmap
flow: Q1: Chef roles baked via Packer

check.a: Running existing CM code during image builds so its logic is reused while deployments become immutable.

drift-remediation-workflows.core: Drift remediation closes the loop between detection and action. Classify drift by risk, revert or adopt each change, combine automated and manual workflows, use event-driven detection to cut exposure from hours to minutes, and tier resources so security drift auto-reverts while stateful or externally owned fields get human or ignore_changes treatment.

first_principles.problem: Drift detection without remediation produces ignored noise and lingering risk.

analogy.title: An immune system with triage
analogy.story: Instant response to dangerous infections, careful judgement for the rest.
analogy.breaks: Bodies self-regulate; you must design the rules.

example.title: Mature setup
flow: Nightly plans open PRs for other drift
Owners adopt or revert within SLA
example.outcome: infrastructure that stays aligned with code.

check.q: What are the two ways to resolve a drift?
check.a: Revert reality to match code, or adopt the change by updating code (and state) to match reality.

generative-iac-llms.core: LLMs make IaC drafting much faster, turning engineers into reviewers. Good prompts with versions, constraints and examples improve output; scaffolding modules, translations and policies is where AI shines; but hallucinations, outdated or insecure patterns and slopsquatting mean every change still flows through validation, scanning, plan review, human judgement and pipeline-only apply.

first_principles.problem: AI increases IaC volume and risk at the same time.

analogy.title: A brilliant but unreliable intern
analogy.story: Great first drafts, but nothing ships without review.
analogy.breaks: Interns learn; models need context every time.

check.q: What's the single biggest rule for AI-assisted IaC?
check.a: Treat generated code as untrusted: it must pass the same automated checks and human review, and only the pipeline applies.

iac-cost-estimation-finops-infracost.core: Cost estimation shifts FinOps left: Infracost maps IaC resources to cloud prices and shows each change's monthly delta in the PR, with usage files covering usage-based costs. Cost policies then add tiered guardrails (thresholds, efficient defaults, tags), so engineers make cost-aware decisions at the cheapest moment, during code review.

first_principles.problem: Cloud costs are invisible until the bill, long after the decisions.
truths: Review time is when changes are cheapest.

analogy.title: Price tags in the shopping cart
analogy.story: Know what it costs before checkout.

check.q: What does 'shift-left' mean for cloud cost?
check.a: Surfacing cost impact during development and review rather than after deployment when the bill arrives.

iac-design-patterns-composition-facade.core: Software design patterns apply to IaC. Composition assembles small modules (Terraform has no inheritance), facades give teams simple intent-based interfaces with org defaults, and dependency inversion has modules receive their dependencies so they work anywhere. Together they form a three-layer stack: resource modules, facades, environment roots.

first_principles.problem: Growing IaC becomes duplicated, coupled and hard to reuse.

analogy.title: Bricks, prefab rooms, houses
analogy.story: Each layer builds on the last with standard connectors.

check.q: Why can't you use inheritance to reuse Terraform modules?
check.a: HCL has no inheritance mechanism; reuse is only through calling modules and wiring inputs and outputs, i.e. composition.

iac-tenancy-models-cell-architecture.core: SaaS tenancy is a trade-off between cost and isolation, and the IaC structure encodes it. Pooling all tenants in one state is simple but has maximal blast radius; a workspace per tenant isolates state but forces lockstep upgrades; cell-based directories give independent state and versions with wave rollouts. Choose per tenant tier.

first_principles.problem: Noisy neighbours and big-bang upgrades threaten multi-tenant reliability.

analogy.title: Apartments, copies, and watertight compartments
analogy.story: From shared walls to sealed bulkheads, more isolation costs more.
analogy.breaks: Buildings don't migrate tenants; you can.

check.q: Why is cell-based architecture considered the gold standard at scale?
check.a: Independent state and versions per cell limit blast radius and allow staged rollouts across tenants.
